carrying-limits-s1.title: A deer herd on an island

carrying-limits-s2.title: The reindeer of St. Matthew Island
carrying-limits-s2.passage: In 1944, 29 reindeer were released on St. Matthew Island, a remote island in the Bering Sea with no wolves or other large predators. The island’s lichens, the reindeer’s main winter food, had built up over centuries into thick mats. By 1963 the herd had grown to about 6,000 animals, and biologists found the lichen mats grazed down and trampled over much of the island. During the severe winter of 1963 to 1964, most of the reindeer starved. A survey in 1966 found 42 animals, and the herd later died out. Lichens grow only a few millimeters a year, so the island’s winter food would take decades to recover.
carrying-limits-s2.source: Invented passage for practice, summarizing published accounts of the St. Matthew Island reindeer, studied by the biologist David Klein (US Fish and Wildlife Service and University of Alaska).

items.q: According to the figure, in about which year did the herd first rise above its carrying capacity?
options: Year 12
Year 6
Year 16
Year 20

why.correct: Find where the herd line first rises above the dashed carrying capacity line.
options: Right: the herd was 640 in year 9 and 1,080 in year 12, crossing the 1,000 line between them.
In year 6 the herd was 300, well below 1,000.
Year 16 is the peak, after the herd had already passed 1,000.
By year 20 the herd had fallen to 600, below 1,000.

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in the herd from its peak of 1,700 in year 16 to 380 in year 22, then give the answer, rounded to the nearest whole percent.

why.correct: Start at the peak: $\frac{380 - 1{,}700}{1{,}700} \times 100 \approx -78\%$. The dieback removed more than three quarters of the herd.

mistakes.why: That is the change in deer. Divide by 1,700 and multiply by 100 for the percent change.
That divides by 380. Divide by the starting value, 1,700.
Start from the peak: (new - old) / old, so (380 - 1700) / 1700 × 100.
Divide by the starting value, 1,700, not by 380.

items.q: After the dieback, the herd levels off near 750, below the original carrying capacity of 1,000. Which explanation fits best?
options: The deer that survived were too old to have young
Heavy grazing hurt the plants, lowering K
Carrying capacity rises after a dieback
Deer prefer to keep their herd smaller after a crash

why.correct: Overshoot can lower carrying capacity by damaging the resources.
options: The herd grows from 380 to about 750, so the deer are reproducing.
Right: overshoot damaged the resources, so the island now supports fewer deer.
The herd levels off lower than before, not higher.
Population size is set by resources, not by preference.

items.q: Which management action would most likely have prevented the overshoot shown in the figure?
options: Adding more deer to the island in year 10
Removing the island’s food plants to slow growth
Removing some deer once the herd neared 1,000
Waiting until year 20 to count the deer again

why.correct: Keeping a population at or below carrying capacity prevents overshoot and dieback.
options: More deer would make the overshoot worse.
Removing food lowers carrying capacity and causes starvation.
Right: keeping the herd near the carrying capacity avoids damage to the plants and the crash.
By year 20 the dieback had already happened.

items.q: Which claim does the passage best support?
options: Wolves caused the reindeer population to crash in 1964
Lichens grow quickly and recovered within a year
The reindeer died out because they were overhunted
The reindeer outgrew their winter food and crashed

why.correct: The passage traces growth, overshoot, food loss and dieback.
options: The passage says the island had no wolves.
The passage says lichens grow only a few millimeters a year.
The passage blames starvation, not hunting.
Right: the herd grew to 6,000, grazed down the lichen and then starved.

items.q: Which assumption is the passage making when it calls the 6,000 reindeer an overshoot?
options: The island could not supply that much lichen year after year
The reindeer would have kept growing without the hard winter
The first 29 reindeer were already too many for the island
Reindeer herds tend to crash after about 20 years

why.correct: Overshoot means resources are being used faster than they are replaced.
options: Right: overshoot means using food faster than it grows back, which the grazed-down lichen shows.
The passage does not assume unlimited growth; it describes damaged food.
The herd grew for years, so 29 was well below carrying capacity.
The passage is about this island’s food supply, not a fixed time span.

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in the herd from about 6,000 in 1963 to 42 in 1966, then give the answer.

mistakes.why: That is the fraction. Multiply by 100: about -99.3%.
That is the change in reindeer. Divide by 6,000 and multiply by 100.
That is the fraction. Multiply by 100 for a percent.

items.q: Which detail best explains why the island could not support a large herd again soon after the crash?
options: The island lies far out in the cold Bering Sea
Lichens grow just a few millimeters a year
The first reindeer were released in 1944
The survey in 1966 counted 42 animals

why.correct: Carrying capacity depends on how fast resources are replaced.
options: Location alone does not explain slow recovery.
Right: slow regrowth of the main winter food keeps carrying capacity low for decades.
The release date does not explain why food is slow to return.
The count shows the crash, not why food stays scarce.

items.q: Which statement best defines carrying capacity?
options: The largest number of offspring one female can have
The number of different species an area can hold
The largest population an environment can support over time
The total mass of food in an ecosystem at one time

why.correct: Carrying capacity: the largest population supportable over time.
options: That is about reproduction, not the environment.
That is species richness.
Right: it is set by food, water, space and other resources.
Carrying capacity is a number of individuals, not a mass of food.

items.q: What happens to a population during dieback?
options: It grows slowly toward carrying capacity
It stays steady, right at its carrying capacity
It moves to a new habitat that has more food
It drops sharply as food runs short

why.correct: Dieback is a sharp decline after overshoot.
options: Slow growth toward the limit is not dieback.
A population at carrying capacity is not crashing.
Moving is migration, not dieback.
Right: dieback is the crash that follows overshoot.

items.q: Which changes would lower the carrying capacity of a lake for a fish species? Select all that apply.
options: A drought that shrinks the lake by half
A wet year that raises the lake’s water level
A rise in the number of insects the fish eat
New underwater plants that shelter young fish

why.correct: Carrying capacity falls when resources or space shrink and rises when they grow.
options: Right: less water means less space and food.
More water means more space and food, which raises carrying capacity.
More food would raise carrying capacity.
More shelter would raise carrying capacity.

items.q: Explain how a goat population on an island can lower the island’s carrying capacity for goats.

why.correct: Overshoot, damage to the resource, lower carrying capacity.

cause.label: Population state
options: grow past the carrying capacity
stay well below the carrying capacity
leave the island

why.1: A population below carrying capacity does not overuse its food.
why.2: If goats leave, they cannot damage the island.

effect.label: Effect on resources
options: eat plants faster than they regrow and expose soil to erosion
plant new trees as they graze
add nutrients that make plants grow faster than they are eaten

why.2: In overshoot, plants are eaten faster than they regrow.

mechanism.label: Result
options: the island can support fewer goats than before
the island can support more goats than before
the carrying capacity stays the same

why.1: Damaged plants and soil support fewer goats, not more.
why.2: Damage to resources lowers carrying capacity.

specific.model: When the goats grow past the carrying capacity, they eat plants faster than they regrow and expose soil to erosion, so the island can support fewer goats than before.

items.q: A wildlife refuge feeds a deer herd extra hay every winter for 20 years, and the herd grows to twice its earlier size. The feeding then stops. Which outcome is most likely?
options: A dieback, as the herd is far above the natural carrying capacity
No change, because the deer are used to the area
Faster growth, because the deer are well fed
The herd stays at its new size for good

why.correct: Remove an added resource and carrying capacity drops back.
options: Right: hay raised the carrying capacity; without it the herd is in overshoot.
Being used to an area does not provide food.
Once the extra food stops, there is less food per deer, not more.
The natural food supply cannot support twice the earlier herd.

items.q: Human ingenuity, such as fertilizer and irrigation, has raised the amount of food the land produces. How does this relate to carrying capacity?
options: It has no effect, because carrying capacity is fixed
It raises the land’s carrying capacity for people
It lowers carrying capacity by adding food
It turns any overshoot straight into dieback

why.correct: Carrying capacity depends on resources, and people can change resources.
options: Carrying capacity changes when resources change.
Right: more food per hectare means the land can support more people, as long as the soil and water last.
Adding food raises carrying capacity.
Raising food supply does not cause a crash by itself.

items.q: A population graph shows a herd rising above a dashed line, crashing well below it, and then rising and falling around a lower level. What does the lower level most likely show?
options: The herd’s biotic potential for growth
The number of species living in the area
A new, lower K after resources were damaged
The highest size the herd could ever reach

why.correct: The level a population settles around is its carrying capacity.
options: Biotic potential is a rate of growth, not a level the herd settles at.
The graph counts one herd, not species.
Right: the herd now settles around a lower level, the new carrying capacity.
The herd once went higher, during overshoot.
